SPCX is a highly vertically integrated disruptor leveraging unrivaled capabilities in launch to establish dominant positions in Global Connectivity and Artificial Intelligence. Because the company's ultimate advantage is rooted in its ability to deliver mass to orbit at greater scale and lower unit cost than any other entity on the planet, if SPCX succeeds in demonstrating key technological and operational milestones in the upcoming, catalyst-rich \~2-3 years without faltering, then we see a path to generating \~\$1 trillion in revenue and \~\$830B in Adj EBITDA in 2031. 1) Existing launch capabilities already market-leading

SPCX is the global leader in orbital launch services. More than any other organization, SPCX has achieved space access at scale, transforming an entire industry. SpaceX designs, manufactures, launches, and operates the world's most advanced rockets and spacecraft. The company safely and reliably transports astronauts, satellites, and other payloads, providing cost-efficient, reliable, and high-cadence access to space for its own purposes as well as for third-party commercial and government customers. As of 1Q26, SPCX has launched a total mass to orbit of approximately 7,400 metric tons with a 99%+ mission success rate across its Falcon rockets. The company has completed approximately 650 orbital space launches, and over 540 of those launches were completed by a flight-proven Falcon rocket. In 2025 alone, SpaceX completed 170 missions across Falcon and Starship vehicles and 159 flight-proven booster launches with a 99%+ success rate on attempted booster recoveries. Specifically, SPCX launched over 2,200 metric tons, representing over 80% of mass to orbit for the world in 2025, continuing a trend that has been in place for multiple years. Importantly SPCX has demonstrated that its rocket technology can be scaled across geographies and launch assets. In 2025, SPCX launched from four primary launch pads in the United States and successfully recovered boosters across seven landing facilities including autonomous drone ships and catch towers based on the vehicle type and mission profile. The company believes that its extensive vertical integration and end-to-end control over the entire value chain, from design to launch to operations, allows it to achieve unprecedented speed and cost efficiency and it is difficult to disagree given the enormity of what SPCX has accomplished in launch. Ultimately, we believe that SPCX's unrivaled launch capabilities represent the foundational competitive advantage that enables all other parts of its business.

text: We see limited competition for Falcon 9's existing launch capabilities – let alone a future Starship. SPCX, competes with launch service providers that transport small, medium, and heavy payloads and astronauts to Earth's orbit and beyond. Participants in this market include established aerospace and defense companies, emerging commercial launch providers, and national space agencies such as United Launch Alliance, a joint venture between Boeing and Lockheed Martin, Arianespace, a French-based aerospace company operating a family of European-developed rockets, and Northrop Grumman, manufacturer of the Cygnus cargo spacecraft. Emerging commercial launch providers include Blue Origin, which has developed launch vehicles intended to compete with the Falcon 9 rocket, and Rocket Lab, which operates in the small-lift launch market but is expanding into medium-lift payloads, as well as other domestic competitors such as Firefly Aerospace and Relativity Space. While SPCX does not typically compete directly for the same missions, national space agencies also provide launch services in their respective markets.

Moreover, the launch services market is characterized by significant barriers to entry, including substantial capital requirements, advanced technological expertise, regulatory licenses and approvals, and established relationships with government and commercial customers. Competition in this market is based on factors that include launch reliability and cadence, payload capacity, mission flexibility, manufacturing capabilities and price. For this reason, while the established aerospace and defense competitors and emerging commercial launch providers may provide launch services at varying degrees of scale, we believe that SPCX holds a meaningful advantage in terms of the breadth, capability, scale, and cadence launch solutions and services. Ultimately, SPCX is the lowest cost, highest reliability, and largest scale player in the existing launch market – even before considering a potentially successful Starship program.

text: SPCX's market-leading existing launch capabilities are rooted in a set of differentiated and hard-to-replicate space assets that took years of innovation to develop. SPCX likes to say that in December 2015, they achieved what many deemed impossible: landing a rocket launched to space back on Earth. But the innovation arc did not stop there. By 2017, SPCX was routinely recovering and reusing the Falcon 9 first-stage booster post-launch, delivering another step-function drop in space access costs via groundbreaking reusability. As of 1Q26, Falcon 9 rockets have demonstrated the ability to refly a first-stage as many as 34 times. Furthermore, since 2020, SPCX's Dragon spacecraft has safely flown 78 crewmembers from 20 countries.
Today, SPCX's existing launch capabilities are supported by a wide range of critical and difficult to replicate assets which we summarize below:

Falcon 9 – Falcon 9 stands as the world's first orbital-class rapidly reusable rocket, fundamentally transforming the economics of space access since its 2010 debut. With approximately 620 orbital launches and an over 99% mission success rate as of 1Q26, it has become the most active orbital launch vehicle in history. The rocket's reusability, recovering and refurbishing both boosters and payload fairings, has reduced the cost per ton to orbit by approximately 85% compared to the historical average of \$18,500 per kilogram. In 2025 alone, Falcon 9 conducted 165 launches, accounting for over half of all global orbital launches while delivering over 80% of mass to orbit. Its in-house developed Merlin engines, which achieve one of the highest thrust-to-weight ratios in operational service, combined with over 530 successful booster landings and more than 540 launches by flight-proven rockets, demonstrate the reliability and maturity of its reusability architecture. As the only U.S.-based launch vehicle certified by NASA for human spaceflight under the Commercial Crew Program, Falcon 9 has successfully launched 19 crewed missions with a 100% success rate, establishing SpaceX as the leader in global space access.

text: Falcon Heavy – Falcon Heavy represents one of the most powerful operational rockets in the world, generating over five million pounds of thrust at liftoff through its 27 Merlin engines across three reusable Falcon 9 boosters. With a payload capacity of approximately 64 metric tons to low-Earth orbit and 27 metric tons to geosynchronous transfer orbit, it fills a critical capability gap for large or high-value payloads while maintaining partial reusability to reduce costs. Importantly, Falcon Heavy has achieved a perfect 100% mission success rate across 11 launches as of 1Q26. The vehicle's sophisticated recovery system enables the controlled landing of its two side boosters and center core, with flown boosters completing 18 total recoveries and 16 reflights, demonstrating an average of 6 flights per booster. Certified for National Security Space Launch in 2019, Falcon Heavy has been selected by NASA for critical missions including the Europa Clipper to Jupiter, Dragonfly to Saturn, and the Nancy Grace Roman telescope. Its unique combination of heavy-lift capability, partial reusability, and proven reliability has made it the vehicle of choice for exploratory missions beyond Earth's orbit while maintaining economic advantages over traditional expendable rockets.

text: Dragon Spacecraft – Dragon spacecraft revolutionized commercial spaceflight by becoming the first privately developed vehicle to deliver cargo to the International Space Station in 2012 and the first to transport humans to orbit in 2020, ending nearly a decade of U.S. reliance on foreign spacecraft. The Dragon cargo variant uniquely combines a 6,000-kilogram launch payload capacity with a 3,000-kilogram return capability, making it the only spacecraft able to return significant amounts of cargo from the International Space Station to Earth for scientific analysis. Dragon's autonomous docking capability via NASA's International Docking System Standard, combined with its reusability after ocean splashdown and refurbishment, has enabled over 30 cargo missions and nearly 15 crewed missions to the space station as of 1Q26. The crew variant's advanced safety features, including eight Super Draco engines for launch escape, touchscreen manual controls, and life support for missions up to nine months, have achieved a flawless safety record in crewed operations. Dragon has pioneered commercial space tourism, supported all of NASA's private astronaut missions, completed the first human spaceflight over Earth's polar regions, and enabled the first-ever commercial spacewalk. Its proven track record of over 50 visits to the International Space Station, combined with recent demonstrations of station altitude re-boost capability, establishes Dragon as the most versatile and reliable spacecraft in commercial operation today.

Landing Zones 1 and 2 enable Return to Launch Site booster recoveries, dramatically reducing turnaround time and costs compared to ocean-based recovery. SpaceX's aggressive expansion plans include constructing a Starship launch pad at LC-39A by end of 2026 and developing Space Launch Complex 37 with two additional Starship pads by end of 2027, culminating in four operational Starship launch pads. The new Gigabay integration facility and continued investment in the Bakery for Starship heatshield tile production demonstrate SpaceX's commitment to vertical integration and rapid operational tempo. This concentration of launch, landing, refurbishment, and manufacturing capabilities in a single geographic region creates unmatched operational efficiency and enables the high-cadence launch operations that have made SpaceX the world's leading launch provider.

While many competitors are trying to develop rocket technologies that are roughly Falcon 9-competitive, SPCX is disrupting its own launch business with the fully and rapidly reusable Starship. As discussed in the prior section, SPCX is already the global leader in launch – yet - Starship, a two-stage super heavy-lift launch vehicle that the company has been flight testing since 2023, further enhances its industry-defining launch offerings. Starship is SPCX's next-generation vehicle that the company expects will dramatically expand its launch capability through full and rapid reusability combined with unprecedented mass to orbit capability. The company believes that Starship is the most powerful launch system ever developed, and we find it hard to disagree. We expect that Starship V3 will be able to carry a payload of 100 metric tons and that future generations could reach 200 metric tons, likely as soon as Starship V4. Moreover, we assume that Starship will be the only vehicle with fully reusable first and second stages, which is critical to reducing launch costs and increasing launch cadence, for many years and the only vehicle to operate in this way at a 100+ metric ton scale for over a decade. Once Starship's launch cadence reaches the thousands annually, we expect launch costs to fall by \~90% per metric ton (from \~\$2,700/ton to \$270/ton) and from there SPCX believes that costs could fall 99%+ vs. the Falcon 9 as launch cadence grows, future generations of the Starship are capable of carrying greater payload, and the company expands opportunities for extreme vertical integration.

Starship V3 is designed to deliver 100 metric tons to Earth's orbit in a fully reusable configuration while enabling rapid turnaround times akin to commercial aviation. Future generations of Starship are being designed to double this payload capacity. To date, SPCX has executed 12 Starship flight tests. text: Full and rapid reusability: Starship's core design innovation is its full and rapid approach to reusability: both stages return to Earth for catch and rapid refurbishment. Raptor engines offer nearly triple the thrust per engine, higher efficiency, and better performance for heavy-lift and deep space missions compared to the Merlin engine used on Falcon 9, according to the company. 3) Falling launch costs open up new growth markets

SPCX believes that space represents the largest economic frontier in human history – and we agree. The company argues that since Earth has obvious limits, it is inevitable that we must build infrastructure and industries in space, expanding human capabilities to improve life on Earth and to establish life beyond. One example of this is SPCX's space-based ‘Connectivity’ infrastructure, also known as Starlink. Another example is AI infrastructure in space, which can utilize the virtually limitless power of the Sun and thereby enable the use of AI as a transformative force for understanding the universe and improving the daily lives of all humans. SPCX believes the convergence of these areas will enable an unprecedented expansion in the global economy, leading to an age of abundance and its innovations and technological advancements will redefine entire industries on Earth, while also creating new ones on the Moon, Mars, and beyond. In this section we help illustrate the falling launch cost algorithm that drives this vision of the future.

SPCX has already demonstrated a history of driving huge reductions in launch costs through the Falcon 9. With the first successful launch of Falcon 1 in 2008, SPCX became the first private company to successfully launch a liquid-fueled rocket to Earth's orbit. In 2010, the commercial debut of the Falcon 9 rocket revolutionized space access by delivering cost efficiency that was unprecedented at the time. For example, according to NASA, the first version of Falcon 9 in 2010 reduced launch cost to approximately \$2,700 per kilogram, which represented a reduction of approximately 85% compared to the historical average launch cost per kilogram of \$18,500. The first version of Falcon Heavy in 2018 further reduced this cost to \$1,400 per kilogram, a reduction of approximately 92% compared to the historical average. SPCX has also further reduced its internal cost of launch through a combination of engineering improvements, manufacturing efficiencies, and economies of scale, most notably through its ability to drive more frequent reuse of rockets, according to the company. Furthering the point, until the 2000s and the introduction of the Falcon 9 rocket, global commercial launch activity averaged 25 to 35 launches per year. As a result, the space industry remained a niche domain with limited ability to support large commercial markets or scaled space-based infrastructure.

4) Launch risks

Being the world's market-leader in launch is not easy – getting to the point where the Starship can be launched thousands of times per year carries significant execution risk. Below we highlight seven execution risks that we think are particularly important to consider, but not insurmountable:

■ Access to launch facilities: To launch thousands of times a year, SPCX needs access to >10 launchpads, in our view. text: Navigating our scenario analysis. The above scenario analysis does not take into account geographical limitations given that there are vast regions of the world in which there are minimal to no subscriber opportunities. The other consideration for a LEO constellation is location density. For example, in rural areas, LEO satellite constellations are likely to offer enough or more capacity than there are subscription opportunities. In those areas, the constellation can serve the entire market with above average performance for the constellation. The challenge is that in urban/suburban areas, there are likely to be far more subscription opportunities to serve relative to the capacity available from the constellation. Hence, we believe the subscriptions for Starlink's broadband constellation will still be heavily skewed to smaller, rural, unserved, and underserved markets relative to suburban and urban markets. In practice, our scenario analysis of effective capacity infers that 95% of subscriptions in the U.S. market will originate in the 40% of households that are in smaller and rural markets when Starlink establishes \~15k V3 satellites. Even with the prospects for 40k V3 satellites, we estimate that 93% of subscriptions will originate from SMRA markets for Starlink. The opportunity to boost broadband subscription opportunities in urban and suburban markets will likely need substantially greater spectrum per spot beam as well as significant enhancements in technology to support better bits per Hz efficiency. One other consideration is the company's TAM is influenced by regulatory approvals and possible geopolitical limitations within each country. For example, Starlink is not operating service in Russia and China, while the company is still pursuing approvals to operate in India.
B) D2D Constellation

The Starlink D2D satellite constellation has \~650 satellites at present that can offer text and messaging services. With the introduction of Starship and the recent acquisition of spectrum in the US, Starlink plans to launch 7.5k of its V2 satellites that will substantially expand capacity and capabilities for end subscribers and create a 5G usage experience.

We see two parallel business cases for the constellation. First, Starlink is likely to continue to offer complementary D2D roaming services on a wholesale and retail basis to the global market. Second, Starlink is looking to leverage its D2D constellation to offer direct mobile services. However, we believe the subscription limitations in urban and suburban markets as well as the importance of high-quality in-building coverage are likely to require a terrestrial component for Starlink to offer a highly-competitive complete mobile solution.

text: We see three possible paths to create terrestrial coverage to offer end-to-end mobile services:

1. Build organically – Execution requires assembling a layer cake of spectrum, constructing or leasing terrestrial cell sites and establishing a full retail go-to-market operation. For reference, Sprint required \~40–50K sites, with lease economics of approximately \$150k-\$250k per cell site per month on a leased tower. SPCX's vertical integration culture supports this approach, but spectrum scarcity, particularly in low-band, complicates a pure-build strategy in the US and could be impractical in many other geographies, including in Europe. The advantages are optimizing long-term margins and full customer-relationship control. The disadvantages are capital intensity, slow time-to-market, and dependence on spectrum auctions that may not deliver the required band mix on management's timeline.

2. Buy a carrier – Acquiring an established carrier represents the fastest route to scale, allowing subscribers, distribution, and ongoing cash flow in a single transaction (referenced in a recent note, Some Thoughts on the Communications Industry Structure). That could be an interesting path, as SPCX relies on cash flow generation from the connectivity segment to redeploy into the broader SpaceX operations. The advantages are speed, immediate cash flow contribution, and reduced execution risk. The disadvantages are acquisition cost, regulatory scrutiny and integration risk associated with operating a traditional carrier. Within this scenario, the decision as to which carrier would best align with SpaceX's forward strategy may depend on how SpaceX wants to pursue TAM. If SpaceX wants to maximize TAM, a Telco with broader fiber reach (especially in urban and suburban areas) can enable a deeper converged service offering across the U.S. market. Also, enterprise operations could also be of interest to extend its reach into the vertical with

3. MVNO – The lightest-capital option would involve a MVNO agreement that would allow SpaceX to offer wireless services using another operator's network. In the US market, the three national MNOs carriers have publicly indicated (see link, link, link) that they are not interested in an MVNO agreement with SpaceX. Historical cable-industry MVNO arrangements demonstrate that such structures can be unlocked when carriers are externally incentivized. There is also the possibility that one of the carriers sees a differentiated opportunity with SpaceX or simply needs incremental revenue to offset other areas of weakness and decides to partner with SpaceX and/or other LEO constellations. Internationally, particularly in markets where spectrum is difficult to acquire, MVNOs may represent the most attractive path, allowing Starlink to layer its satellite differentiator atop borrowed terrestrial capacity.

We believe the most probable outcome is a hybrid, geography by geography strategy: build or buy in select markets where spectrum and economics support it, MVNO in markets where carrier partnerships are accessible, and pure D2D and wholesale in markets that are too small or restrictive for direct entry.
4) Impact to wireless and broadband markets

Consistent with the history of the communications ecosystem, Starlink is likely to receive some degree of cooperation as well as competition from the telecom and cable incumbents. In broadband, Starlink will be competing for subscriptions in both the residential and business markets, while cable and telecom companies may still resell Starlink solutions for connectivity to specific underserved verticals. For example, Comcast offers its enterprise customers to integrate Starlink satellite capabilities into their connectivity solutions. T-Mobile is currently reselling Starlink D2D services under its T-Satellite branded solution, while also entering into a joint venture (for spectrum and IP) with the other carriers to promote additional D2D competition. Starlink also faces direct competition from emerging constellations from AST SpaceMobile and Amazon LEO that are in the process of launching their satellites into orbit, albeit currently well behind Starlink's established constellation.

The wrinkle in the D2D market is that the enthusiasm for monetizing valuable coverage assurance from their customers has faded from the low level of usage being reported by both T-Mobile and independent firms, including Ookla. Although Ookla is reporting a nearly 25% increase in global D2D connections between July 2025 and March 2026 as Starlink has expanded into new geographies, monthly usage was disclosed as generally less than 1% with 0.46% of Speedtest users in the US connecting to D2D satellites. The US market also leads the world in D2D connections at nearly 46% of the usage. As Starlink migrates to its V2 platform with greater continuity of coverage and substantially greater capacity, the D2D category should be able to offer a more compelling case for coverage assurance in markets with well built terrestrial mobile networks, such as in the US, and expand use cases in markets with a lot of rural sprawl and under-built mobile infrastructure.

text: 2) X platform real-time data integration

The deep, proprietary integration between Grok and the X platform establishes a highly differentiated vertical AI ecosystem where real-time data ingestion serves as a foundational engine for model training and context integration. By securing exclusive access to a continuous stream of public discourse, Grok bypasses the critical data collection bottlenecks that limit traditional off-the-shelf models developed by industry peers. This live data pipeline allows the AI to ground its output in real-time global events, providing difficult to match freshness and contextual relevance that standard static training datasets cannot replicate. Furthermore, the diversity of human conversation and multi-perspective commentary hosted on X serves as an empirical foundation for Grok's truth-seeking objective. This steady influx of real-time commentary ensures that the model remains dynamically aware of breaking developments and shifting public sentiment as they unfold. Consequently, this proprietary integration creates a powerful competitive moat that structurally separates Grok from legacy AI systems operated by their competitors. Ultimately, the resulting ecosystem synergy enhances both model performance and platform engagement, driving high-value use cases for consumer and enterprise applications alike.

3) Grok has yet to take off in a meaningful way

SPCX's Grok model primarily competes with other leading US frontier models such as Google's Gemini across the major cloud platforms. Management believes Grok's access to real-time data (via X.com) is a key differentiator and will benefit enterprise GTM. The company's orbital AI compute vision (SpaceX, Feb. 2026) is a credible yet execution-dependent extension of the company's core advantages in launch, satellite manufacturing, Starlink networking, and vertically integrated hardware. Is space-based AI infrastructure inevitable? Critical to the company's view is a belief that current advances in AI across both training and inference will require an amount of electricity that cannot be met with terrestrial methods. Therefore, in the long term, space-based AI is the solution to the widening gap between compute demand and power availability. In other words, “try getting the permits [to cover Nevada in solar panels]...it’s harder to scale on ground than it is to scale in space” (A Cheeky Pint, Feb. 2026). text: 2) Addressing constraints in the terrestrial AI market

The constructive case for orbital AI is that it addresses the most constrained parts of the terrestrial data center stack: power, cooling, permitting, grid interconnection, and physical build time. These satellites will be enabled by solar power (free and clean), Starship deployment, Starlink optical networking, and high-volume satellite manufacturing. Early AI satellite power targets of 100 kW per satellite, compute-density targets of 80-120 kW per ton, and an aspirational deployment rate of 100 GW per year would require \~1M metric tons per year to orbit and the company aims to deploy up to a million satellites (FCC, Jan. 2026). Accordingly, Starship is central to the company's ambitions as it will be the only fully reusable system designed to carry 100+ metric tons to orbit, which is the style of launch architecture needed for 200 kW-class satellites and gigawatt-scale deployment.

However, although there are proof points, none of this has been done at a commercial scale. Starcloud, an orbital data center startup, has shown that orbital AI compute is technically possible at demo scale, launching Starcloud-1 with an NVIDIA H100 and claiming the first LLM training/fine-tuning in orbit (LinkedIn, Nov. 2025). Launched by a Falcon 9 and the size of a small refrigerator, the H100 ran inference on a Google Gemma model and trained Andrej Karpathy's nano-GPT on the complete works of Shakespeare (X, Dec. 2025). This technical milestone proved that a data-center-class GPU could survive launch, operate on solar power in orbit, and execute LLM inference and small-scale training workloads. However, scalable power density, thermal rejection, high-bandwidth networking, maintenance/replenishment, and economics remain unproven.

The technology building blocks increasingly exist, the question remains whether SPCX can integrate them at data center scale and at a cost that outperforms terrestrial alternatives. 3) Economics attractive on the non-chip infrastructure

We view orbital AI as potentially disruptive to the non-chip portion of the AI data center stack first, and to the full cost-per-token stack only later if Terafab materially reduces accelerator costs. In the interim, AI satellite economics are primarily an ex-chip infrastructure advantage, though our analysis demonstrates that the cost curve remains an engineering challenge. The economics can become attractive on the non-chip infrastructure layer if Starship cadence and satellite manufacturing scale materialize. However, the processor layer still remains a critical cost bucket, so orbital AI does not become a full-stack cost advantage unless SpaceX also reduces accelerator cost through Terafab, proprietary chip design, or materially better utilization. The company is targeting 90% value capture through its supply chain derisking effort via Terafab.

We estimate that 30% of terrestrial AI data center costs are dedicated to construction/shell/MEP/grid interconnection, with the remaining 70% dedicated to chips and other critical IT equipment. Therefore, SpaceX's current cost advantage could remain structurally bounded if it only reduces the construction, power, cooling, and deployment layers while still utilizing higher cost, NVIDIA-class silicon. Our work suggests that relatively aggressive assumptions around launch cost reduction, satellite manufacturing learning curves, solar array costs, and thermal simplification are needed to justify the longer-term costs. Our illustrative analysis assumes a 200 kW AI satellite, 2-ton launch mass, 100 kW/ton specific power, 190 GPU-equivalent chips, and 10% chip infant mortality & non-compute power distribution, yielding 180 kW effective delivered power after adjustment. On that basis, the model estimates ex-chip, ex-Terafab total satellite cost of \$8.5M in 2029E, falling to \$6.5M in 2030E and \$5.8M in 2031E, equivalent to \$47/W, \$36/W, and \$32/W upfront, or \$9.4/W/year, \$7.2/W/year, and \$6.4/W/year over a five-year useful life.
4) Orbital AI Risks

Given this is a technology that has never been attempted at scale before, there is a possibility that the architecture is economically fragile once real-world losses materialize. These losses could include liquid cooling loop mass, additional shielding, dedicated radiator mass, radiation-hardening premiums, solar cell cost inflation versus terrestrial benchmarks, and failure related derating. Thermal management may become an important technical gating item. SpaceX's AI1 concept describes a deployable liquid radiator with redundant pumping loops, suggesting that the company is already contemplating active thermal systems rather than purely passive radiative cooling – though this could be describing a chip-level heat transport loop which works simultaneously with a radiative rejection mechanism. Finally, we note that there are several orbital governance considerations, including debris, collision-avoidance, deorbit, spectrum, astronomy, and optical brightness.

It is well understood by now that the semiconductor industry is facing persistent shortages across logic and memory driven by insatiable AI demand. Simultaneously, the memory market is experiencing an unprecedented surge in demand for HBM and advanced DRAM. The company's Launch segment pioneered full reusability to provide affordable access to orbit, while its Connectivity segment operates the world's largest satellite constellation to deliver high-speed internet globally. Following its acquisition of xAI, SpaceX has also established a dedicated AI segment that integrates frontier models like Grok with massive terrestrial and orbital compute infrastructure.
Investment strategy

We rate shares of SPCX a Buy due to the following points: 1) Unrivaled launch capabilities right now and for the foreseeable future; 2) Unique capability of scaling space infrastructure and unlocking trillion-dollar market opportunities (Orbital AI and Starlink); 3) Extreme vertical integration, which reinforces the company's ability to drive costs down, throughput up, and deliver at a scale at which no competitor can replicate; and 4) Differentiated margin and growth profiles.
Valuation

We derive our \$200 base-case price target for SPCX using the average of three valuation methods: 1) 2027E growth adj. multiples (EV/Revenue/Growth and EV/EBITDA/Growth) for the “Trillion-Dollar Comps” (a basket of similar trillion-dollar+ market caps); 2) sum-of-the-parts (SOTP) valuing Space, Connectivity, and AI separately using 2027E growth adj. multiples (EV/Revenue/Growth and EV/EBITDA/Growth) for industry-specific comparable companies; and 3) 2030E comparable company multiples (EV/Revenue and EV/EBITDA) for the “Trillion-Dollar Comps” (a basket of similar trillion dollar+ market caps).
Risks

Risks to our thesis, which could impede the shares from reaching our price target, include headwinds to the launch segment which reference the failure to demonstrate rapid reusability on Starship, lack of launch infrastructure, and regulatory headwinds from the FAA and other government organizations. The failure to rapidly gain market share in Starlink mobile, as well as demonstrate the ability to create AI orbital satellites capable of compute, also presents risks to SPCX.
